name: Body language / presence training
lead: Body language or presence training is the deliberate practice of nonverbal behaviour, such as an open stance, steady eye contact, slower movements and an upright carriage, so as to come across as more confident, warm and commanding. In appearance communities it is treated as the part of looks that moves: two people with the same face can leave different impressions depending on how they hold and present themselves.[1][2]

Wikipedia defines body language as nonverbal communication through posture, gestures, facial expressions, eye movement, touch and use of space, mostly occurring without conscious awareness, and notes that open, relaxed postures and warmth are linked to impressions of trust.[1] Research on thin slices of behaviour, begun by Nalini Ambady and Robert Rosenthal in 1992, found that observers form reasonably accurate impressions of interpersonal traits from clips of a few seconds, which is the scientific backdrop for the idea that a person's bearing is read almost instantly.[14]

The idea reached a very wide audience through power posing: in a 2012 TED talk Amy Cuddy proposed that holding expansive poses makes people feel more powerful.[2][12] Later research found a reliable effect on how people feel but no reliable effect on hormones and an unclear effect on behaviour.[2][5] On looksmax.org, members write guides on 'charismamaxxing' that pair body language with voice tone and humour, and threads on reading interest and indifference in others.[3][4]

chain: Practise open posture, eye contact and calm movement
Others read more confidence and warmth
Stronger first impression and social presence
angle.text: Practitioners use body language training to change the impression their appearance gives, standing taller, holding eye contact and moving more slowly so that their looks are read alongside confidence. The practice costs nothing and is done alongside posture work, grooming and style.

paras: Body language is the set of physical behaviours that accompany or replace speech. Wikipedia lists posture, gait, gestures, facial expressions, eye movement, touch, breathing and the use of space among them, and notes that unlike sign languages it has no grammar and so is not a language in the linguistic sense.[1] Practitioners of presence training treat these behaviours as trainable habits: a slumped, hurried or closed bearing can be replaced with an upright, unhurried and open one.

In appearance terms the idea is that physical looks and bearing are perceived together. Someone who stands tall, moves calmly and meets others' eyes is described as seeming more attractive and more at ease than the same person hunched and fidgeting. The practice costs nothing and is typically done alongside posture work, grooming, fitness and clothing choices.

The formal study of body movement in communication is called kinesics. Anthropologist Ray Birdwhistell coined the term in 1952, filmed people in social situations, and proposed a unit of movement he called the kineme by analogy with the phoneme.[11] He estimated that words carry no more than 30 to 35 percent of a conversation's social meaning, concluded that kinesic displays have no universals, and disliked the popular term body language; Paul Ekman disputed the no-universals claim in his work on facial expressions.[11][1] Gestures, Birdwhistell held, are polysemic and cannot be decoded in any absolute way.[1]

Edward T. Hall introduced proxemics in 1966, dividing interpersonal distance into intimate, personal, social and public zones.[1] Hall's framework underlies advice about how close to stand and how much space to occupy.

Albert Mehrabian's 1967 studies are the source of the widely repeated 7%-38%-55% figures, which assign words, tone and facial expression shares of how much a speaker is liked when feelings are being communicated. Wikipedia notes that the figures combine two separate studies that used a single spoken word and photographs, involved only female participants and addressed only positive versus negative feelings, and that Mehrabian himself said the equations apply only to communication of feelings and attitudes.[13] The figures are nonetheless often cited as proof that most of a message is nonverbal.[13][4]

Reports note that leaning forward and nodding suggests openness, folded arms are often read as a closed mind, and relaxed hands suggest confidence.[1] Firm handshakes are said to improve the accuracy of first impressions.[1] Head tilt can be read as interest or suspicion, and posture and gait can reflect mood.[1]

Eye contact is often read as sincerity in workplaces, but meaning varies by culture, with prolonged gaze seen as a challenge or anger in some cultures.[1] The same gesture can differ in meaning: arms akimbo may signal relaxed confidence in Western countries but is considered rude in Bali.[1] A family-medicine review on cross-cultural care lists attitudes toward personal space, eye contact and body language among the areas where expectations differ between cultures.[6] Kinesics scholarship likewise notes that interpretations vary by culture, so misreading is a risk in intercultural settings.[11]

Ambady and Rosenthal's 1992 meta-analysis introduced the term thin slice for a brief sample of expressive behaviour. In 1993 they showed raters 2-, 5- and 10-second clips of teachers' nonverbal behaviour and found the ratings closely matched those of people with substantial contact, with clip length making no significant difference.[14] Wikipedia reports that thin-slicing works best for observable interpersonal traits such as dominance or shyness and less well for traits such as conscientiousness or intelligence, and that in this literature physical attractiveness mattered less when expressive behaviour was visible.[14]

Practitioners cite this literature to argue that bearing is evaluated quickly and that changing it changes the impression made. Malcolm Gladwell's book Blink popularised the idea of snap judgments to a general audience, though Wikipedia notes that some of its supporting claims have been criticised.[14]

In 2010 Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap published a Psychological Science study of 42 participants reporting higher testosterone and lower cortisol after expansive poses, and suggested benefits for job interviews and negotiation.[2] Cuddy's 2012 TED talk reached a very large audience, with about 47 million views by 2017, and her 2015 book Presence reached number three on the New York Times advice best-seller list in February 2016.[2][12]

A 2015 replication by Eva Ranehill and colleagues found an effect on felt power but not on hormones, risk tolerance or behaviour.[2] In 2016 Carney stated that she no longer believed the effect was real, and Simonsohn and Simmons argued that it disappeared once selective reporting was accounted for.[2] Cuddy and colleagues published a 2018 analysis of 55 studies arguing for evidential value for effects on feelings and has continued to defend the research.[2][12] A 2022 meta-analysis of 128 studies by Körner and colleagues reported reliable effects on thoughts and feelings, no effect on physiological measures and an unclear behavioural effect, noting that few studies included a neutral-posture control.[2] Critics have also pointed out that many experiments compared expansive poses only with slouched ones, so they cannot show that expansive poses themselves help.[2]

A looksmax.org guide to charismamaxxing argues that charisma can make a difference to dating, jobs and friendships even for tall, conventionally attractive men, and splits it into body language, voice tonality and humour.[4] It cites the 7%-38%-55% split attributed to Mehrabian.[4][13]

Another thread, by a member who says he has studied body language for months, lists signs he associates with interest, such as preening, frequent eye contact and nervous behaviour, while noting that no single sign is conclusive.[3] Further threads cover mirroring and social-skills guides.[7][8] Outside the forum, a 2012 Hacker News discussion titled 'How Studying Body Language Changed the Way I Socialize' drew 188 points and 94 comments, showing the same self-improvement interest in general tech communities.[10]

Scholars disagree whether body language is universal, and Mehrabian's 7%-38%-55% split is widely debated.[1][13] Wikipedia states there is no scientific evidence that nonverbal cues reliably detect lies, though some law enforcement agencies still use them.[1] A 2021 BJPsych International review observed that people may be less skilled at reading others' faces and body language than they think.[9]
No studies found for presence training as a looks-related intervention. Related laboratory research on power posing and thin-slice judgments is summarised above.[5][14]

lore.intro: Body language is discussed on looksmax.org as part of 'charisma' and social skills, often alongside voice and humour, with members sharing guides on how to project confidence and read others.[3][4]

claims.claim: Body language and tone carry most of the meaning in communication
claims.believers: A charisma guide on looksmax.org states that 7% of communication is words, 38% tone and 55% body language.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that Mehrabian's percentages combine two small studies and that he limited them to communication of feelings; Birdwhistell's kinesics holds that gestures cannot be decoded in any absolute way.[13][1]

claims.claim: Consistent signs in someone's body language reveal interest or indifference
claims.believers: One forum author lists preening, frequent eye contact and nervous behaviour as signs of attraction, advising that context matters.[3]
claims.experts: A 2021 review notes people may be worse at reading others' body language than they assume, and thin-slice research finds accuracy is best for observable traits such as dominance.[9][14]

claims.claim: Expansive poses make you feel and act more powerful
claims.believers: Power-posing advocates, led by Amy Cuddy, argue that posing can make people feel more powerful and confident.[2][12]
claims.experts: A 2022 meta-analysis of 128 studies found reliable effects on thoughts and feelings but none on physiological measures, with behavioural effects unclear.[5]

claims.claim: Power poses raise testosterone and lower cortisol
claims.believers: The 2010 study by Carney, Cuddy and Yap reported such hormone changes after expansive poses.[5]
claims.experts: A 2015 replication found no hormone effect, and Carney later said she no longer believed the effect was real.[5]

claims.claim: Mirroring someone's body language builds rapport
claims.believers: Forum members describe mirroring as an effective social technique.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's body-language article describes warmth and open posture as signals of trust but does not report trials of deliberate mirroring.[1]

claims.claim: First impressions are formed within seconds from bearing and expression
claims.believers: Practitioners hold that stance and eye contact shape how quickly others judge them.[4]
claims.experts: Thin-slice studies found impressions from 2- to 10-second clips matched those of well-acquainted raters for some interpersonal traits.[14]

claims.claim: Gestures mean the same thing everywhere
claims.believers: Guides on gesture reading are often written as general rules.
claims.experts: Eye contact, gestures and personal space carry different meanings across cultures, and Birdwhistell concluded kinesic displays have no universals.[1][11]

card.summary: Training stance, eye contact and pace to look more confident; the research supports felt confidence more than outcomes.
card.note: Meanings of gestures vary by culture; power-posing hormone effects were not replicated.

quick.overview:
Body language training means practising open posture, steady eye contact and calmer movement to project confidence.

Power-posing research found reliable effects on how people feel, but not on hormones, and behavioural effects are unclear. Gesture meanings also vary across cultures.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners say changing outward behaviour alters how others read confidence and may feed back into mood. Studies support the mood link more than the others.
quick.risks: Low risk. Cross-cultural misreading of gestures and eye contact is the main caveat noted in references.
